The researchers also found that the models struggle to explain the humor behind a joke, often providing superficial explanations that don't capture the complexity of human humor. The study concludes that while large language models have made significant progress in generating humor, they still have a long way to go in truly understanding and replicating human humor.

Hello everyone, my name is Daniel Rotem and I'll be presenting my work, "Finding the Sweet Spot: Analysis and Improvement of Adaptive Inference in Low Resource Settings", which was done in Professor Roy Schwartz's lab at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem. Adaptive inference is a method for reducing the inference time of large language models. We rely on the fact that real-world data varies in complexity. Therefore, we can use low-capacity models for simpler tasks and high-capacity models for more complex tasks. Our goal is to find the optimal model capacity for a given task. We analyze the performance of models with different capacities on various tasks and identify the sweet spot where the model's performance is optimal. We also investigate how to improve the inference time of the models by using techniques such as knowledge distillation and model pruning. Our results show that adaptive inference can significantly reduce the inference time of large language models, making them more practical for real-world applications.

Title: Transfer Learning for Dissonance Detection: Addressing the Rare Class Challenge
Cognitive dissonance is a psychological phenomenon where individuals experience discomfort or tension when holding two conflicting beliefs or actions. In the context of language, dissonance detection is crucial for understanding human communication and behavior. However, detecting dissonance in text is a challenging task due to the rarity of dissonant instances and the complexity of linguistic and contextual factors. This paper presents a transfer learning approach to address the rare class challenge in dissonance detection. We propose a novel framework that leverages pre-trained language models and fine-tunes them on a dissonance-labeled dataset. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the task, outperforming traditional machine learning methods. The proposed framework demonstrates the potential of transfer learning for dissonance detection and provides a foundation for further research in this area.
